intro: The spell checker reads your draft against the dictionary-en en_US Hunspell word list, with every lookup and suggestion produced in the page by nspell. It names the dictionary it uses so its findings can be checked rather than trusted.
content:
Type or paste a draft and this spell checker splits it into word-shaped tokens, decides which tokens are worth looking up, and asks the en_US Hunspell dictionary about the rest. Every lookup happens in the page: the dictionary files are imported by the browser when this tool is opened, and nothing you paste is sent anywhere.

The dictionary is a real one, and the page names it. The word list is the dictionary-en package, version 4.0.0, a Hunspell en_US dictionary derived from SCOWL and licensed MIT AND BSD (about 562 KB unpacked). The lookups and the suggestions come from nspell (MIT, about 41 KB unpacked), imported lazily alongside the affix and dictionary files. No word list was typed from memory into this tool.

- Skip rules, on by default and individually switchable: ALL-CAPS tokens such as API and NASA, tokens containing digits such as utf8 or ISO8601, and camel-case brand shapes such as iPhone or eBay.
- Always skipped, whatever the switches say: six code-like span types (web addresses, email addresses, Markdown links, file names with known extensions, snake_case and SCREAMING_SNAKE identifiers, and anything inside backticks), tokens shorter than two letters, and non-Latin scripts.
- Words to accept: a free-text field where names, products and jargon are added once and skipped for the rest of the session.
- Suggestions: up to six per unknown word, computed for the first 40 distinct unknown words; later words are listed with a note that no suggestions were computed.
- Reporting: unknown words grouped by spelling with a count and up to 12 occurrence positions, capped at 300 distinct words, with Copy report and Download.

The engine is deliberately thin, and that is what makes the result checkable. Tokens are cut with a Unicode pattern that keeps utf8 and ISO8601 whole instead of slicing them into pieces. A hyphenated token is looked up whole first, then each part of at least two letters, so well-know is reported as know, which is where the error actually is. Lookups normalise curly apostrophes to straight ones and lower-case the token. Suggestions are generated by walking single-character edits — deletion, transposition, replacement and insertion — and keeping only the candidates that exist in the dictionary, which is why receive appears for recieve. The extracted offsets point at the exact characters, so each finding can be located in the original text.

- The dictionary is American English. colour, organise and centre are reported as unknown and offered color, organize and center; add the forms you intend to the accept field, or run the Consistent Spelling Checker to treat US and UK forms as a style choice rather than an error.
- Names, brands and jargon are unknown to any general dictionary. Racira, Kubernetes and localhost are reported like misspellings, and the accept field exists for exactly that.
- It checks spelling alone. There is no grammar, punctuation or meaning in the engine, so form and from are both correct words to it.
- Suggestions come from edit distance, not intent: a typo can receive suggestions that share its shape rather than its sense.
- The report is capped: 300 distinct words listed, 12 occurrences per word, and suggestions computed for the first 40.

Use the summary to see the size of what was actually judged: words checked, tokens skipped, suggestions computed. Work through repeated spellings first, add the proper nouns your document depends on to the accept field, and then hand the text to the Homophone Confusion Detector for the word confusions a dictionary cannot resolve.
howTo: Paste or type a draft; the dictionary loads once for this page and lookups begin when it is ready.
Add the names, products and jargon you use to Words to accept so the real errors stand out.
Leave the three skip switches on unless you want acronyms, digit-bearing tokens or brand shapes checked as well.
Work down the unknown words table from the most frequent, then Copy report or Download the list.
whenToUse:
Use this spell check as the first mechanical pass over a draft, then hand the text to the tools that answer different questions. When the question is which variant to use rather than whether a word exists, the {{consistent-spelling-checker|Consistent Spelling Checker}} compares US and UK forms across the whole document, and the {{homophone-confusion-detector|Homophone Confusion Detector}} covers the pairs a dictionary cannot judge at all, such as their and there.

If the spelling is clean and the sentence still carries a mechanical slip, the {{grammar-checker|Grammar Checker}} runs its published list of checks over the same text.

faqs.q: How does a hyphenated word get reported?
faqs.a: The whole compound is looked up first. If it is unknown, each part of at least two letters is looked up separately and only the rejected parts are reported, so well-know is reported as know rather than as the entire token.

faqs.q: What do the three skip switches change?
faqs.a: They control ALL-CAPS acronyms such as API, tokens containing digits such as utf8, and camel-case brand shapes such as iPhone. All three are skipped by default, and switching one off sends those tokens to the dictionary.

faqs.q: How many suggestions are computed, and for which words?
faqs.a: Suggestions are computed for the first 40 distinct unknown words, up to six each. Any word after that is listed with a note that no suggestions were computed, so a long list of odd tokens cannot stall the page.

faqs.q: Why is a product name flagged as a misspelling?
faqs.a: Because a general dictionary does not contain private names, brands or jargon. Racira, Kubernetes and localhost are unknown words to it; adding them to Words to accept skips them for the rest of the session.

faqs.q: Which code-like spans are never looked up?
faqs.a: Six kinds: web addresses, email addresses, Markdown links, file names with known extensions, snake_case and SCREAMING_SNAKE identifiers, and anything inside backticks. They are excluded before any lookup, because a URL is not a spelling.

intro: The Homophone Confusion Detector checks 44 documented pairs — your and you're, its and it's, their and there, then and than — and only reports a spelling when the surrounding words make the other one implausible.
content:
Homophones sound alike and are spelled differently, which is exactly the mistake a spelling checker cannot see: your and you're are both real words, so both pass a dictionary. This homophone confusion detector looks at the words around each candidate instead of the candidate alone, and it publishes the homophone pairs it knows so the claim is checkable. The context rules are narrow by design: word confusion between two real words, which no dictionary can resolve.

- The list holds 44 pairs, one rule per pair. Examples include its / it's, your / you're, their / there / they're, to / too / two, then / than, whose / who's, affect / effect, lose / loose, passed / past, quiet / quite, accept / except, advice / advise, peace / piece, principal / principle, stationary / stationery, complement / compliment, cite / site / sight, brake / break, lead / led, everyday / every day, weather / whether, desert / dessert, hole / whole, wait / weight, threw / through, right / write, which / witch, steal / steel, meat / meet, one / won, sea / see, sun / son, tail / tale, weak / week, aloud / allowed, bare / bear, throne / thrown, mail / male, plain / plane, board / bored, flour / flower, pair / pear and waist / waste.
- One entry is a misspelling rather than a pair: alot is always reported as a lot, with no context needed.
- Each finding carries the word as written, the spelling the context calls for, the pair, a one-line reason, and a snippet of about 30 characters either side so the sentence can be judged without hunting for it.
- A pair summary counts the findings per pair, so the habits that repeat are visible at the top.

Every rule is a construction, and the patterns are built by four helpers so the lookaround order cannot be got wrong by hand: after places context in a leading? trailing lookahead, before places it in a leading lookbehind, around uses both, and exact matches the word with no context at all. The whole match is always the flagged word itself, so the reported offset points at the word rather than at the phrase around it. Matching is case-insensitive. When a rule suggests a replacement, the writer's capitalisation of the first letter is preserved, so Your going is corrected to You're going rather than you're going. Findings are sorted in document order and capped at 400, which a pathological input cannot exceed.

- The tool has no idea what you meant. It knows these 44 constructions, not your sentences, so a pun, a line of dialogue, an idiom or a regional usage can put a flagged form where the rule does not expect it.
- Pairs whose contexts are identical are not checked at all. Where read and red both fit the same surroundings, a rule would fire on correct sentences, so no rule exists.
- The list is finite. A confusion not on it is not reported, and absence of a finding is not proof that every homophone in the draft is right.
- Nothing is edited. Each finding is a question to answer; the draft changes only when you change it.
- The per-pair summary is the part to read when a finding repeats, because a repeated construction is usually one typing habit rather than many mistakes.

Run the detector on the text you are about to send rather than on a first draft, because a clause you are still restructuring can lose the construction that fired. Copy report gives you the word, the fix, the pair and the reason in one list, and the pair summary at the end shows which pairs actually mattered instead of leaving you with a bare total.
howTo: Paste the draft; the 44 pair rules scan the whole text as you type.
Read each finding against its sentence: the word, the suggested form, the pair and the reason are all listed.
Check the pair summary for habits that repeat, since those are the ones worth rewriting first.
Copy report or Download, then re-run after editing because a rewritten clause can remove the construction that fired.
whenToUse:
Use this detector on any draft where a wrong real word would embarrass you, and pair it with the checks that cover the neighbouring faults. The {{apostrophe-error-finder|Apostrophe Error Finder}} handles dropped and stray marks in contractions and possessives, and the {{spell-checker|Spell Checker}} covers words that are not in the dictionary at all.

When the confusion is a matter of sentence structure rather than a word pair, the {{grammar-checker|Grammar Checker}} runs a published list of mechanical checks over the same text.

faqs.q: What do the four pattern helpers do?
faqs.a: They build each rule's lookaround: after puts the context in a trailing lookahead, before puts it in a leading lookbehind, around uses both, and exact needs no context. The whole match is always the flagged word, so offsets stay precise.

faqs.q: Why does the detector stay silent on some homophones?
faqs.a: Because no context rule would be reliable where both spellings fit the same surroundings. Those pairs are excluded rather than guessed at, since a rule that fires on correct sentences trains you to ignore the useful findings.

faqs.q: What is in a finding besides the suggested spelling?
faqs.a: The word as written, the pair it belongs to, a one-line reason, and a snippet of roughly 30 characters either side. The reason is what lets you agree or overrule in a second.

faqs.q: Is there a cap on how many findings are listed?
faqs.a: Yes, 400 findings in document order. The cap protects the page from a pathological input; the pair summary still shows which pairs produced them.

faqs.q: Can a rule fire on a sentence that is actually correct?
faqs.a: Yes, and the page says so. Deliberate puns, dialogue, idioms and regional usage can put a flagged form where a rule does not expect it. The detector reports and never edits, so overruling a finding costs nothing.

intro: The punctuation checker runs 11 mechanical checks over the character stream — spaces in the wrong place, punctuation doubled, brackets and quotes that do not pair up, paragraphs with no full stop — and labels each one as an error or a style note.
content:
Punctuation faults divide into two kinds: the ones visible in the characters and the ones that depend on meaning. This punctuation checker concentrates on mechanical punctuation, because those are the faults a machine can find without pretending to understand the sentence. Eleven checks run and all eleven are listed on the page, split into five errors and six style findings.

- Errors: a space before a full stop, comma or other mark; a missing space after punctuation; unmatched brackets, whether round, square or curly, counted by type; an odd number of straight double quotation marks or a mismatch between curly opening and closing quotes; and a paragraph that ends without any terminal punctuation.
- Style findings: the same mark repeated, an ellipsis written with other than exactly three dots, a hyphen with spaces on both sides standing in for a dash, two or more hyphens in a row, a space before a closing bracket, and a space after an opening one.
- Every finding carries the rule label, the issue in words, a mechanical fix where one exists, the character offset and a short context snippet.
- Per-rule counts are shown in a grid, so one rule firing eleven times reads differently from eleven rules firing once.

The checks read the character stream directly, and the near-misses are carved out deliberately, because a checker that fires on correct text is one you stop reading. A comma inside a grouped number such as 1,000 never counts as a missing space, and neither does a colon in a time such as 10:30. A shared list of 27 abbreviations — al, approx, cf, dept, e.g, est, etc, fig, ibid, i.e, inc, jr, ltd, mr, mrs, ms, no, pp, prof, sr, st, vs, vol and their relatives — keeps the full stop in e.g. and i.e. from being treated as a sentence end, and initials such as J.K. are excluded the same way. A window of 60 characters around a match is tested for web and email shapes, so nothing inside a URL can fire. Quotation marks are counted by type: straight marks are counted together, curly openings and closings separately, and an apostrophe is never counted as a quotation mark at all. Findings are sorted in document order and capped at 200, and the per-rule counts reflect that capped list.

- Comma usage is out of scope by design: a comma splice, the Oxford comma, restrictive clauses and dialogue punctuation all depend on what the sentence is doing, and a pattern cannot judge them.
- A missing apostrophe is a word-level issue and belongs to the Apostrophe Error Finder, not here.
- Deliberate punctuation is reported at style severity so it can be overruled — a four-dot ellipsis, an em dash run or a raised eyebrow question mark is a choice, not automatically a fault.
- The bracket checks count characters, not nesting: an unmatched brace is reported with the side that has no partner, but a correctly paired set that crosses another pair is not judged.
- Nothing is rewritten. Each mechanical fix is a suggestion next to the finding, and the draft changes only when you apply it.

Use the counts as a map rather than a score. One rule firing repeatedly is a single habit and usually a quick fix; a spread across many rules is a draft that needs a read-through for the marks. Copy report and Download give you the whole list with context, which is the fastest way to work through a document that has been through several editing passes.
howTo: Paste your text; the 11 checks run as you type and each count appears in the grid.
Fix the error findings first, since spaces and unmatched marks are unambiguous.
Read the style findings in context — a deliberate ellipsis or dash run is yours to keep.
Work through the paragraphs flagged without end punctuation, then Copy report or Download the list.
whenToUse:
Use this as the mark-level pass, after the wording is settled and before you look at anything larger. Word-level faults that are not marks belong to the {{apostrophe-error-finder|Apostrophe Error Finder}}, and a lower-case sentence start or a stray capital belongs to the {{capitalization-checker|Capitalization Checker}}.

When the marks are clean and the sentences still carry mechanical slips, the {{grammar-checker|Grammar Checker}} covers repeated words, article agreement and unmatched brackets over the same text.

faqs.q: What does the error and style split mean?
faqs.a: Five checks are errors: a space in the wrong place, a missing space, unmatched brackets, unbalanced quotation marks and a paragraph with no end punctuation. Six are style notes, including repeated marks, a non-standard ellipsis and dash conventions, and they are yours to overrule.

faqs.q: How does the checker treat e.g. and initials such as J.K.?
faqs.a: A shared list of 27 abbreviations keeps their full stops from counting as sentence ends, and initials are excluded the same way. The same abbreviation list is shared with the Capitalization Checker, so the two tools agree.

faqs.q: Why is 1,000 not reported as a missing space?
faqs.a: Because a comma followed by a digit is a grouped number. A colon in a time such as 10:30 is excluded by the same guard, so the missing-space check stays quiet on correct text.

faqs.q: How are quotation marks counted?
faqs.a: Straight double marks are counted together, curly opening and closing marks separately, and an apostrophe is never counted as a quotation mark. An odd number of straight marks, or a curly mismatch, is reported as unbalanced.

faqs.q: What is the finding cap?
faqs.a: 200 findings in document order, and the per-rule counts reflect that capped list. The cap keeps a pathological input from producing an unreadable report.

intro: The Apostrophe Error Finder works from a published list of 27 spellings that only exist without their apostrophe — dont, isnt, couldnt — plus checks for stray marks, doubled marks, decade apostrophes and mixed straight and curly styles.
content:
The most common apostrophe mistake is not a misplaced mark but a missing one: a dropped apostrophe in one of the everyday contractions leaves a plausible string of letters, so the eye reads straight past it. This apostrophe error finder handles that fault with a closed list of 27 spellings that are only correct with the mark, and the list is printed in full on the page so the claim can be checked line by line.

- Missing apostrophe in a contraction: the published forms include dont, doesnt, didnt, isnt, arent, wasnt, werent, hasnt, havent, hadnt, couldnt, wouldnt, shouldnt, aint, oclock, youre, theyre, theres, thats, whats, heres and wheres.
- Three entries are real words on their own — im, ive and lets — so they are marked as needing evidence and only fire when the next word proves the contraction.
- Plural possessive: a word followed by 's and then a plural verb such as are, were, have, has, had, do, does or did is reported with the plural form.
- Decade apostrophe: 1990's is reported at style severity, because the modern plural convention is 1990s while the possessive use is accepted as written.
- Stray apostrophe: a mark at the end of a word, before punctuation or at a line end, with no partner and no word after it.
- Doubled apostrophe: two marks in a row, including a straight and a curly one side by side.
- Mixed styles: a document using both the straight ' and the curly ’ gets one typography finding, because the mix shows in typeset output.

The evidence logic is what keeps the ambiguous three quiet. Before flagging lets, the engine checks whether a subject-looking word sits immediately before it; when the word starts a clause, or when it is preceded by a lead-in such as and, but, now or please, the rule then requires a proven follower — a verb or determiner from a published list — so lets you and me go is reported while the plan lets you save is not. The same shape applies to im and ive. The plural-possessive rule pairs its subject test with the plural verb list, so a possessive that is genuinely singular is left alone. Every finding carries the character offset, a context snippet and a suggested fix, capitalisation preserved. The report is capped at 200 findings in document order, and the page shows the size of the published list it used.

- Context homophones are not checked here. its and it's, whose and who's, and they're, their and there need the surrounding words, so they belong to the Homophone Confusion Detector.
- A possessive that is simply missing cannot be found. In the students books, a machine would need to know that students is a noun and books is what they own, so no rule exists for it.
- Plural possessives are accepted exactly as written: the dogs' toys is never rewritten as dog's.
- The list is closed. A form outside the 27 published spellings is not guessed at, so a clean result means those listed faults are absent rather than that every apostrophe is correct.
- The mixed-style finding is whole-document and fires once, not once per mark.

Run the finder on the whole document rather than paragraph by paragraph so the mixed-style check has enough to compare, and start with whatever form repeats, because one fix removes many findings. Copy report and Download give the list with the suggested fix, which is the fastest way through a draft that has lost its marks to copy and paste.
howTo: Paste the draft; the published list and the other five checks run as you type.
Fix the missing-apostrophe findings first, starting with whichever form repeats.
Check the im, ive and lets findings in context — those rules need the next word as evidence.
Read the decade and mixed-style findings, then Copy report or Download the list.
whenToUse:
Use this finder when the marks in a draft have been through copy and paste and need checking, and use its siblings for the faults it hands over. Contractions that need context — its and it's, whose and who's, their and there — are the {{homophone-confusion-detector|Homophone Confusion Detector}}'s job, and mark placement around brackets and quotes is the {{punctuation-checker|Punctuation Checker}}'s.

When the apostrophe is right and the capitalisation around it is not, the {{capitalization-checker|Capitalization Checker}} covers sentence starts, the pronoun I and documented names.

faqs.q: How does the tool keep the plan lets you save out of the findings?
faqs.a: The ambiguous forms need evidence. If a subject-looking word sits immediately before lets, or the word starts a clause with a lead-in such as and or now, the rule then demands a proven follower like a verb or determiner; only then is the contraction reported.

faqs.q: Why is 1990's only a style finding?
faqs.a: The plural decade convention is 1990s with no apostrophe, so the form is flagged at style severity. The possessive use, as in the 1990's biggest hits, is accepted as written and never rewritten.

faqs.q: Why does the finder not check its and it's?
faqs.a: Those spellings are homophones rather than a missing mark: both are real words, and only the surrounding words say which is meant. The Homophone Confusion Detector owns that pair, and this tool stays quiet on it rather than duplicating a worse rule.

faqs.q: What triggers the mixed apostrophe styles finding?
faqs.a: A document that contains both the straight ' and the curly ’. Each is correct on its own, but switching between them is visible in typeset output, so the mix is reported once as a typography note.

faqs.q: How many spellings does the published list contain?
faqs.a: 27, and the whole list is printed on the page. Three of them — im, ive and lets — are conditional because they are real words on their own; the rest are always reported when they appear.

intro: This capitalization checker runs five published checks — lower-case sentence starts, the pronoun i, day, month, language and nationality names, ALL-CAPS words and capitals inside a word — and keeps the two style checks separate from the three errors.
content:
Capitalization errors are quiet ones. A lower-case word after a full stop does not look wrong inside ordinary sentence case, which is why it survives a careful read and why a mechanical scan for proper capitalization is worth running. This capitalization checker runs five published checks, and the two treated as style — all caps runs and capitals inside a word — are kept apart from the three treated as errors.

- Sentence starts lower-case (error): a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark followed by a lower-case word, or a lower-case first word of a line.
- Lower-case i as the pronoun (error): i on its own and inside i'm, i've, i'll and i'd.
- Lower-case day, month, language or nationality (error): 81 documented names, with words that are also ordinary English — march, may, august, polish and their relatives — excluded.
- Word in all capitals (style): three or more capitals, minus a published acronym allowlist such as API, URL, JSON, PDF, SEO, CEO and USA.
- Capital inside a word (style): minus a brand list that includes iPhone, macOS, YouTube, GitHub, JavaScript, eBay and others.

The sentence-start rule scans raw text rather than parsed sentences, and that is deliberate: the shared sentence splitter needs a capital letter after the full stop to recognise a sentence at all, so a lower-case start would be invisible to it. The pattern is instead the error itself — a terminator, a space, then a lower-case word — with the two cases that are not errors carved out: abbreviations such as e.g. and i.e., and initials such as J.K. The abbreviation list of 27 forms is shared with the Punctuation Checker, so one tool cannot treat a full stop as a sentence end while the other does not. A deliberate lower-case start after an ellipsis is left alone, because that pattern is a style choice in fiction and dialogue. The name rule reads the long weekday and month names from the platform's Intl data at run time rather than typing them into the engine, and takes the language and nationality lists from the same curated source the Proper Noun Checker uses. Findings are sorted in document order and capped at 200, with per-rule counts shown beside each check.

- Country, continent and planet names are not checked here. They belong to the Proper Noun Checker, which also finds a name the document writes two different ways.
- Names that are also ordinary words are never flagged on their own in either tool: a sentence about a march or a polish is not a sentence about a month or a country.
- The acronym allowlist and the brand list are finite and published. A legitimate initialism that is not on the list will be reported as a style finding, and the fix is to leave it.
- The checker has no grammar and no meaning. It can see that a word is capitalised the wrong way, not that the sentence is wrong.
- Nothing is rewritten automatically; each finding shows the suggested form and leaves the draft untouched.

Use the counts to see which habit a draft has. A single rule firing repeatedly is one fix; a spread across the two style rules usually means the draft needs a decision about emphasis rather than a tidy-up. Copy report and Download produce the findings with a suggested form for each, so the fixes can be made in one pass.
howTo: Paste your text; all five checks run as you type and each count appears beside its check.
Work through the sentence-start findings first — they usually cluster around one editing seam.
Check the pronoun i findings, including the contractions i'm and i've.
Read the ALL-CAPS and inner-capital findings as style questions, then Copy report or Download the list.
whenToUse:
Use this checker on any draft that has been edited in pieces, since a lower-case sentence start is often the scar of a rewrite. Where the capitalisation problem is a name written two ways, the {{proper-noun-checker|Proper Noun Checker}} handles it with a documented lexicon and a consistency check.

When the capital is right but the mark beside it is not, the {{punctuation-checker|Punctuation Checker}} covers unmatched brackets, doubled marks and a paragraph with no full stop.

faqs.q: Why does the sentence-start rule scan raw text instead of parsed sentences?
faqs.a: Because the shared sentence splitter needs a capital after the full stop to see a sentence boundary at all, so a lower-case start would never be recognised. Scanning for the error pattern directly is the only way to find it.

faqs.q: How many names does the name rule hold?
faqs.a: 81 day, month, language and nationality names. The weekday and month names are read from the platform's Intl data at run time, and names that are also ordinary English words, such as march and may, are excluded from the rule.

faqs.q: Why is march never flagged as a month name?
faqs.a: Because it is ambiguous. A march is also a walk and a march is also music, so flagging the lower-case form alone would invent errors. The tool would rather miss a case than report one.

faqs.q: Is an ALL-CAPS word treated as an error?
faqs.a: No, it is a style finding. Emphasis, initialisms and headings are legitimate uses; the published acronym allowlist keeps everyday initialisms quiet, and the remaining findings are yours to overrule.

faqs.q: Why is GitHub not rewritten?
faqs.a: Because the internal capital is part of the brand name. A list of known brand forms — GitHub, iPhone, macOS, YouTube, JavaScript, eBay and others — is exempt from the inner-capital rule, so a correct name is never corrected.

intro: The Proper Noun Checker holds 248 documented names across seven kinds and finds both lower-case forms and names a draft writes two different ways. Its unknown-name list is reported, never corrected.
content:
A proper noun checker is useful and dangerous in equal measure, because a name the tool does not know is not a mistake. This one draws that line clearly: it checks 248 documented names, runs a name consistency check across the forms your document uses, lists the capitalised words it does not recognise instead of correcting them, and publishes the count so the scope can be judged.

- The lexicon holds seven kinds of name: 7 long weekday names and 12 long month names read from the platform's Intl data at run time, plus 8 continents, 8 planets, 39 languages, 54 nationalities and 120 countries from curated lists shipped with the tool.
- 19 of the names are also ordinary English words — Turkey, May, March, August, Earth, Mercury, Chile, China, Georgia, India, Japan, Jordan and their relatives — and those are never flagged on their own.
- The consistency check compares capitalised and lower-case forms of the same word when both appear away from a sentence start, and reports the lower-case occurrences against the capitalised form.
- The unknown list shows up to 20 capitalised words that are not in the lexicon, most frequent first, explicitly marked as never corrected.

The case check scans tokens and compares them against two lookup structures: a lower-case map for single-word names and a phrase map for multi-word names, which are matched with spaces or hyphens between the parts, so a lower-case north America is caught against South America's neighbour in the list. Nineteen ambiguous names are excluded before any comparison, because the turkey was dry is a sentence about dinner. For every other lower-case token that matches a documented name, a finding carries the form found, the documented form and the kind of name. A capitalised token that is not in the lexicon is not treated as an error; it is counted, and the most frequent ones are listed as unverified so the part of the draft the lexicon could not see is visible. The consistency check builds a map of forms per lower-case word, ignores any occurrence at the start of a sentence and any ALL-CAPS token, and only fires when the same word appears in both a capitalised and a lower-case form; a short stopword list keeps ordinary function words out of it. Findings are capped at 200.

- The lexicon is a curated list, not a gazetteer. Towns, companies, characters and new brands are outside it, which is the honest limit of a fixed list.
- Ambiguous names are never flagged on their own, so a genuine lower-case Turkey or China in a sentence about the country can pass unnoticed.
- A name written only in lower case, with no capitalised occurrence anywhere, is not detected by the consistency check — the check needs both forms in the text.
- The unknown list is capped at 20 entries and is never treated as a mistake, so it is reading material rather than a findings list.
- Multi-word matching covers documented multi-word names only; an unknown two-word name is not phrase-checked.

Read the output as two questions rather than one: is this documented name lower-case, and does my draft write each name the same way twice? The first is answered by the lexicon, the second by your own text. Where a name appears in two forms, the majority form is usually the intended one, so start there and bring the outliers into line. Copy report and Download give you the findings and the unknown-name list together, which is what settles a naming decision across a long document.
howTo: Paste your draft; documented names and repeated capitalised words are checked as you type.
Read the findings first: each shows the form found, the documented form, the kind of name and the reason.
Study the consistency findings closely — they are about your own text rather than the lexicon.
Scan the capitalised words not in the lexicon and check those spellings by hand, then Copy report or Download.
whenToUse:
Use this checker when a document repeats its own names and needs them to agree — a report, a manuscript, a set of product pages. Case rules that are not name lists belong to the {{capitalization-checker|Capitalization Checker}}, which covers sentence starts, the pronoun I and everyday name classes.

When a name is spelled two ways because of a US and UK convention — colour beside color, centre beside center — the {{consistent-spelling-checker|Consistent Spelling Checker}} answers that question, and the {{spell-checker|Spell Checker}} covers words that are not in any dictionary.

faqs.q: How many names are in the lexicon and where do they come from?
faqs.a: 248 names across seven kinds: 7 weekday and 12 month names read from the platform's Intl data at run time, plus 8 continents, 8 planets, 39 languages, 54 nationalities and 120 countries from curated lists shipped with the tool.

faqs.q: Why is the lowercase chile in a recipe not flagged?
faqs.a: Because 19 names are also ordinary English words and are marked ambiguous. Chile joins Turkey, May, March, China, Jordan, Mercury and the rest; the tool would rather miss a case than report the wrong one.

faqs.q: How does the consistency check avoid flagging a sentence's first word?
faqs.a: Every token is marked as sentence-initial when the gap before it contains a terminator or a newline, and those occurrences are ignored. ALL-CAPS tokens are ignored too, so a heading cannot make a lowercase form look like an inconsistency.

faqs.q: What are the capitalised words not in the lexicon?
faqs.a: Names the curated list does not contain. Up to 20 are listed most frequent first, and the page states that nothing there is corrected. It is the honest measure of how much of the draft the lexicon could not see.

faqs.q: Does it check multi-word names such as South Korea?
faqs.a: Yes, for documented multi-word names. Those are matched as phrases with spaces or hyphens between the parts, so a lower-case spelling of a known country is caught alongside the single-word names.

intro: The Number Format Checker scans a document for numeric tokens, works out how each one is punctuated, and reports ten kinds of inconsistency — from mixed decimal separators to unit spacing — before offering a one-convention rewrite.
content:
A report that writes 1,234.56 in one paragraph and 1.234,56 in the next asks every reader to interpret two conventions at once, and an international reader may read them as different values. This number format checker scans a document, works out how each number is punctuated, and reports the genuine inconsistencies in plain language — the decimal separator, the thousands separator, and the rest of the conventions listed below — because number consistency is a property of the whole document.

- Mixed decimal separators: both a comma and a full stop used as the decimal mark.
- Mixed thousands grouping: both marks used to group digits.
- Ambiguous values such as 1.500, which is fifteen hundred under grouping and one and a half under a decimal reading.
- Irregular grouping: any grouping that is not the standard three-digit pattern, with Indian lakh and crore grouping labelled informational.
- Ungrouped large numbers of five digits or more, which are hard to check at a glance.
- Percent spacing: 50% in some places and 50 % in others.
- Currency placement: symbols appearing both before and after amounts.
- Mixed currencies in one document, reported so the amounts are not compared without a conversion rate.
- Unit spacing per unit: 5kg beside 5 kg.
- Number ranges using both a hyphen and an en dash.

Each numeric token is matched by one pattern that allows a leading currency symbol or ISO code, a sign, grouping separators of comma, full stop, apostrophe, space or the narrow spaces, an optional decimal part, an optional percent sign and an optional unit from a curated list of about 55 entries covering length, mass, volume, time, screen units, temperature, data, frequency and power. The parser then tests two readings: every separator is grouping, or the last separator is decimal. When both readings are legal, as with 1.500, the token is reported as ambiguous and resolved as grouping for the value column, and the interpretation table shows the reading that was used so nothing is decided silently. Irregular grouping, ungrouped numbers, percent and currency placement, mixed currencies, unit spacing and range dashes are detected across the whole document rather than per token, so each is reported once. The rewrite walks the parsed numbers and rebuilds them in one of three conventions — US and UK with 1,234,567.89, European with 1.234.567,89, or SI and French with narrow spaces — preserving currency symbols, signs, percent signs and units exactly where the author put them. Numbers written without separators and four digits or shorter are left alone, because regrouping a year into 2,026 changes what the sentence says.

- The rules are heuristic and carry no locale knowledge. The tool cannot know which convention your document intends; it reports the mixture and lets the rewrite apply the one you choose.
- Ambiguity is reported rather than resolved. The value column picks the grouping reading for display, and the finding says both readings are legal.
- The unit list is curated. A unit outside it is not checked for spacing consistency, and a recognised symbol can appear in a context that is not a measurement.
- Whole-document checks report once each, so they tell you that a mixture exists rather than listing every instance.
- The rewrite changes digit punctuation only. It never converts currencies, never regroups years or small counts, and never touches the words around a number.

Use the checker before publishing anything assembled from several sources or written by someone using a different locale. Copy rewritten text or Download applies one convention to the figures while leaving every other character as the author wrote it, and the interpretation table is the audit trail if a number was read differently from how you meant it.
howTo: Paste the document that contains numbers; the scan runs as you type.
Read the issues list first, since each finding names the kind of problem and quotes the context.
Check the interpretation table for any number marked ambiguous or irregular and confirm the value column matches what you meant.
Choose a convention under Rewrite numbers in, then Copy rewritten text or Download and compare it with the original.
whenToUse:
Use the checker on documents that mix sources: a report assembled from several contributors, a translation handed between teams, or a dataset description written in another locale. It is also the fastest way to audit a document for the specific ambiguity of a number such as 1.500.

When a single value needs to be rendered correctly for one locale rather than audited across a document, the {{number-locale-formatter|Number Locale Formatter}} shares the same parsing rules, and the {{locale-date-formatter|Locale Date Formatter}} covers the equivalent conventions for dates. When the mixed convention is a spelling rather than a figure, the {{consistent-spelling-checker|Consistent Spelling Checker}} answers that question the same way.

faqs.q: Why does the interpretation table show 1.500 as fifteen hundred?
faqs.a: Because both readings are legal and the table has to pick one for its value column. The tool marks the token ambiguous and reports that a decimal reading is possible in other locales; nothing is silently corrected.

faqs.q: Which numbers are left untouched by the rewrite?
faqs.a: Numbers written without separators and four digits or shorter, such as years and small counts. Regrouping 2026 into 2,026 would change the meaning, so the rewrite leaves them exactly as written.

faqs.q: How is Indian grouping such as 1,23,456 treated?
faqs.a: It fails the standard three-digit pattern, so it is reported as irregular grouping with an informational note, because lakh and crore grouping is valid in locales that use it.

faqs.q: Which units does the checker recognise?
faqs.a: A curated list of about 55 units covering length, mass, volume, time, screen units, temperature, data, frequency and power — for example kg, mm, px, GB, °C and %. Spacing is checked per unit, so 5kg beside 5 kg is a finding.

faqs.q: Does the checker convert between currencies?
faqs.a: No. When more than one currency appears it reports that fact so the amounts are not read as directly comparable, but no exchange rate is applied and no value is converted.

intro: The Consistent Spelling Checker compares 95 published US and UK pairs, plus three stem-matched families, and reports the mix rather than the spelling, because both forms are correct English.
content:
US and UK spellings are both correct; what reads badly is a document that uses one variant in the heading and the other in the paragraph. This consistent spelling checker exists for that problem and not for correctness, which is why its verdict is always about the document rather than about a word: it reports spelling consistency across variant spellings.

- 95 listed pairs are checked and reported even when the document is consistent, because then they are evidence of which variant the writer chose: color and colour, center and centre, defense and defence, catalog and catalogue, gray and grey, jewelry and jewellery, and the rest of the published list.
- The -ize and -ise family is matched on the shared stem, so organize against organise fires on any word with that shape, not only the listed ones.
- The -yze and -yse family does the same for analyze against analyse.
- Sixteen published stems cover the doubled-consonant family — cancel, channel, dial, equal, fuel, jewel, label, level, marvel, model, quarrel, shovel, signal, total, travel and tunnel — so traveled beside travelled is detected without collapsing every double letter blindly.
- Verdicts: consistent US, consistent UK, mixed, or no variant words present.
- The families table shows each family's US and UK forms, the rule that matched, and whether it is mixed.

Every token of two or more ASCII letters is classified by four rules, and the rule that matched is carried into the report: listed pairs are looked up in two maps, one per variant; the stem families are matched by two regular expressions, one for the yze and yse shape with a stem of at least three letters and one for the ize and ise shape with a stem of at least four; and the doubled-consonant family matches a published stem followed either by the extra l and a suffix or by the suffix directly. The stem-matched families are kept only when both shapes appear in one document, because using traveled throughout is not evidence of anything, while the listed pairs are always kept. The analysis counts occurrences on both sides, reports which variant the document leans on, and lists the mixed families separately, since a mix is the thing a reader notices. Copy report and Download give the whole picture, which is the useful thing to hand to a co-author or an editor when the question is which convention a publication uses.

- The pair list is finite, and the stem families cover suffix patterns only. A variant outside those shapes is not compared.
- Pairs whose meanings have drifted apart are deliberately excluded: check and cheque, tire and tyre, curb and kerb, draft and draught, and storey and story are different words now, not variants of one another, so a document is never told to change them.
- The tool makes no correctness claim and does not choose for you. A consistently British document needs no changes, and neither does a consistently American one.
- Token matching is ASCII, so words in other scripts are not compared for variants.
- The verdict is a document property: paste the whole text rather than a paragraph, or the answer describes only the excerpt.

Paste the whole document, read the verdict first, and treat a consistent result as finished. When the result is mixed, choose the variant the document leans on and bring the outliers into line, then re-check, because a family drops out of the report once only one form remains. The list is also the place to settle a house-style question before the draft is shared rather than after an editor has changed half of it.
howTo: Paste the whole document, not a paragraph, because consistency is a document-level property.
Read the verdict first — a consistent result needs no changes at all.
If the verdict is mixed, open the families table and look at the rows marked mixed.
Bring the outliers into line with the variant the document leans on, then Copy report or Download the outcome.
whenToUse:
Use this checker when a document has more than one author or has been through several revision passes, which is when variants drift. When the problem is a word the dictionary does not contain at all, the {{spell-checker|Spell Checker}} is the right tool, and when the question is whether a name is written two different ways, the {{proper-noun-checker|Proper Noun Checker}} answers it from a documented lexicon.

When the mixed convention is a figure rather than a word, the {{number-format-checker|Number Format Checker}} reports decimal and grouping inconsistencies in the same document-level way.

faqs.q: What do the four rule labels mean?
faqs.a: Each finding is tagged with the rule that matched: listed for a published pair, ize-ise and yze-yse for the two stem families, and ll-l for the doubled-consonant family. The label tells you how the word was matched, so a finding is never a black box.

faqs.q: Why are check and cheque not compared?
faqs.a: Because their meanings have drifted apart. Check and cheque, tire and tyre, curb and kerb, draft and draught, and storey and story are different words now rather than variants, so they are excluded and a document is never told to change them on this tool's account.

faqs.q: Why are the stem-matched families only reported when mixed?
faqs.a: Because using traveled throughout is not evidence of anything, while using traveled and travelled in one draft is. The listed pairs work the other way round and are reported even when consistent, since then they show which variant the writer chose.

faqs.q: What are the sixteen stems for?
faqs.a: They cover the doubled-consonant family, from cancel to travel. Matching a published stem is deliberate: collapsing every double letter would pair words that are not variants of each other at all, such as filed and filled.

faqs.q: Does the tool decide which variant I should use?
faqs.a: No. It reports the lean and the mixed families and leaves the choice with the writer and the publication. A consistently British document and a consistently American one are both finished results.
